passage: Eshaan here. My flatmate Chinmay was on the sofa, jaw set, thumbs flying, when I brought tea. A clip was going around of a shopkeeper shouting at a customer, and hundreds of people were tearing into him in the replies. Chinmay had a draft open: three lines, each nastier than the last. He looked ready to post. Then he stopped, scrolled up, and searched for the longer video. I saw him watch it twice. "The start is cut off," he said, mostly to himself. "The customer was pushing him." He deleted the draft and wrote one line asking people to wait for the whole clip. Whether he felt embarrassed or just calmer, I couldn't say. He drank the cold tea and put the phone down.

qa.q: What was going around online that had Chinmay typing?
qa.a: A clip of a shopkeeper shouting at a customer was going around.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have stopped and searched for the longer video?
qa.a: He seems to have started wondering whether he knew the full story. Eshaan cannot say if he then felt embarrassed or simply calmer.

qa.q: How could Chinmay challenge behaviour he thinks is wrong without joining a pile-on?
qa.a: Check the whole story first, use facts and stay proportionate, as with the single line asking people to wait for the whole clip. Asking whether he would say it in person also helps.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper have experienced the hundreds of replies?
qa.a: Probably as frightening and hurtful, being torn into by strangers over a clip with the start cut off. A request to wait for the whole clip might come as a relief.

grounding: Righteous anger at a pile-on: pausing to check the full story before joining, and choosing a proportionate, factual response instead.

passage:
Newsroom note from the social media desk, Thursday

This morning a video went round of a school principal in Pune scolding a student. Within an hour, thousands were calling for the principal's arrest. Elizabeth, our newest trainee, drafted a post for our page: "Shameful! This man should never teach again." She was angry, and it came from a good place.

Before she posted, I asked two questions: do we know what happened before the clip starts, and would we say this to his face? She paused, then rang the school.

The full clip showed the student had just shoved a younger child down the stairs. The scolding was sharp but not cruel.

Elizabeth went red. "I almost joined a mob."

We posted a short factual report instead, with both clips. I told her the instinct to defend a child was right; the rush was the problem. She has asked to write the verification checklist for the team.

Ira, desk editor

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's draft post say?
qa.a: "Shameful! This man should never teach again."

qa.q: What did Elizabeth feel when she learned the full story?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and shaken, going red as she realised she had almost joined a mob.

qa.q: What did Ira's two questions help Elizabeth do?
qa.a: They made her pause and check the full story, so the team posted a proportionate, factual report instead of joining the pile-on.

qa.q: How might the principal have been affected if Elizabeth's post had gone up?
qa.a: The principal could have faced even more hatred and threats for a moment that, in full, was sharp but not cruel.

grounding: The note shows a young trainee who feels righteous anger at a pile-on and nearly joins it, then pauses to check the full story and responds with facts and proportion.

passage:
Diary. Pooja. Sunday night, feeling a bit sick with myself.

This afternoon everyone was sharing a video of a woman yelling at a delivery rider outside a café in Bandra. The comments were brutal: her face, her clothes, her company name. I was furious for the rider. I typed "hope she loses her job, disgusting person" and my thumb was over Post.

Then Ayesha sent me a longer version. The rider had knocked her elderly mother over with his bike and was driving off. She was still wrong to scream the things she did. But it wasn't the whole story.

Would I have said "disgusting person" to her face? Never.

I deleted my comment. Instead I wrote one line under Ayesha's post: "Longer clip here. Yelling was wrong, but so is this pile-on."

Three people called me a sellout. I'm okay with that.

qa.q: What did the longer video show?
qa.a: That the rider had knocked the woman's elderly mother over with his bike and was driving off.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when she typed the comment?
qa.a: Pooja felt furious and righteous on the rider's behalf, and later felt sick and ashamed about nearly posting it.

qa.q: What went right in how Pooja handled it?
qa.a: She paused, checked the fuller story, asked whether she'd say it in person, and posted a proportionate line instead of joining the pile-on.

qa.q: How might the woman in the video be affected by the pile-on?
qa.a: She could face threats to her job and safety over one moment, when the full story was more complicated.

grounding: The diary shows someone who feels righteous anger at a pile-on and nearly joins it, then pauses to learn the full story and challenges the mob with facts and proportion.
